transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-09-24 18:42 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-09-25T01:42:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 3.014 degrees and its azimuth is 266.753 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 6.78 degrees and its azimuth is 103.997 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 96.97 percent illuminated, 159.91 degrees from the Sun, and 385592.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—very likely.

A 96.97%-illuminated Moon is essentially a waxing/waning gibbous and is bright enough to be visible in daylight under clear skies. At only about 6.8° altitude it will be low, so the main difficulties are haze, trees/buildings, and the bright near-horizon sky—not lack of lunar brightness.

Your geometry is especially favorable:

- The Sun is very low in the west (azimuth ~267°).
- The Moon is low in the east-southeast (azimuth ~104°), almost opposite the Sun.
- That puts the Moon in a relatively darkened part of the sky compared with looking near the Sun, and it should stand out better as sunset approaches.

Look low toward the east-southeast, roughly a little south of due east, with an unobstructed horizon. It may appear pale white against the blue sky rather than dramatically bright. Because it is so low, act promptly: it will be vulnerable to horizon obstruction and atmospheric extinction, though it should remain visible for a while as the sky darkens.

Do not use binoculars or a telescope while searching anywhere near the Sun; unaided-eye searching in the opposite direction is fine.
